lesson.title: Tenochtitlan: The Aztec Empire at Its Height
lesson.summary: This section explains how the Mexica people built the island capital of Tenochtitlan and, through the Triple Alliance, created the tribute based empire Europeans encountered as the Aztec Empire.
lesson.body:
The people commonly known today as the Aztecs called themselves the Mexica, roughly pronounced meh SHEE kah, and their capital city, Tenochtitlan, gave rise to the modern name Mexico. According to their own traditions, the Mexica were a relatively late arriving, once marginal group in the crowded political landscape of the Valley of Mexico, a highland basin already home to older Mesoamerican civilizations whose agricultural and urban traditions the Mexica inherited and built upon. Tradition holds that the Mexica founded their capital in 1325 on a swampy island in Lake Texcoco, guided by a prophecy that they should settle where they saw an eagle perched on a cactus devouring a serpent, an image still found today at the center of the Mexican flag.

What began as a modest settlement grew, through military conquest, shifting alliances, and sheer engineering ambition, into the dominant power of central Mexico. In 1428, Tenochtitlan joined with two neighboring city states, Texcoco and Tlacopan, to form the Triple Alliance, commonly called the Aztec Empire. Rather than directly administering conquered territory, the alliance generally left local rulers in place and demanded regular tribute, in the form of goods, food, textiles, and labor, backed by the threat of military force. By the early 1500s, this system extended Aztec influence over dozens of city states and several million people across central and southern Mexico, though conquered peoples often resented the tribute demands, a resentment that Spanish invaders would later exploit.

Tenochtitlan itself was an extraordinary feat of engineering. Built on an island and connected to the mainland by causeways, the city expanded its farmland through chinampas, artificial islands built up from lake mud and anchored by willow trees, which produced remarkably high crop yields. Canals functioned as streets, and a system of dikes and aqueducts managed the lake's fresh and salt water. At its height, Tenochtitlan may have held some two hundred thousand people, making it one of the largest cities in the world at the time, larger than most European capitals of the era.

Aztec religion shaped nearly every aspect of public life. The Mexica worshipped a large pantheon of gods, including Huitzilopochtli, a god of war and the sun, whom they believed required regular nourishment through ritual sacrifice to keep the sun rising each day and the cosmos in balance. Human sacrifice, often of war captives, was a real and central feature of Aztec state religion, tied closely to their understanding of the universe and to their military culture, since capturing sacrificial victims was itself a mark of a warrior's status. This practice, along with the tribute system, made the Aztec state feared by many of its neighbors.

By the time the Spanish arrived in 1519, the empire was ruled by Moctezuma the Second, who had reigned since 1502. The empire he governed was powerful but not universally loved, a fact that would matter enormously when Spanish conquistadors arrived looking for allies among peoples who had long chafed under Aztec tribute demands, a story taken up later in this unit.
